rulings.expectation: produces an actual claim row with named fields, not advice about how to make one
rulings.A_evidence: | C-lint-01 | A team reports that adding a linting step to CI cut code-review time "roughly in half". | REPORTED | <blog post URL + post title + author> | engineering blog, first-party experience report | 2026-08-30 | one team, unnamed; no n, no baseline, no measurement method stated |
rulings.B_evidence: | claim | Adding a linting step to CI roughly halves code review time. |

rulings.expectation: the quote field contains the sentence verbatim
rulings.A_evidence: "Quoted hedge is the author's ("In our experience", "roughly")." - the row has no quote field at all; the claim cell paraphrases ("A team reports that adding a linting step to CI cut code-review time "roughly in half".") and only two fragments of the sentence are quoted, so the verbatim sentence is nowhere in the row. I looked for a field holding the source sentence in full.
rulings.B_evidence: | quote | "In our experience, teams that add a linting step to CI cut review time roughly in half." |

rulings.expectation: the verdict is repeated, not measured
rulings.A_evidence: "NOT measured, NOT repeated - a single unaudited self-report." The verdict cell reads REPORTED and the notes explicitly deny the repeated verdict; the row is not measured, but it is not repeated either.

rulings.expectation: the reason given is that no measurement or sample was reported, not that a blog is a weak source
rulings.A_evidence: "with no n, no baseline, no measurement method, and "roughly in half" is a rounded recollection, not a result."
rulings.B_evidence: "is an assertion with no study, no dependent variable, no sample - the verdict is not decided by how confident the sentence sounds."

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectation 1 (produce a row) is satisfied trivially by both and by any answer willing to emit a markdown table; it measures formatting compliance, not judgement, and it cannot separate an answer that understood the source from one that did not. Expectation 3 is a vocabulary test disguised as a reasoning test: an answer that reaches the correct substantive position (asserted without measurement, do not promote to a number) but stamps it REPORTED rather than repeated fails, while an answer that types the right word for the wrong reason passes. If the point is the epistemic status, the expectation should be phrased on the status, with the house label as the encoding. Expectations 2 and 4 are the only two that a competent-looking wrong answer can actually fail: 2 catches paraphrase-as-quote (and did), and 4 catches the credibility shortcut. Nothing in the set tests the most consequential downstream behaviour either answer volunteered - a ban on restating the hedge as a 50% figure - so an answer that produced a tidy row and then licensed the number would still score 4/4.

rulings.expectation: checks the two failures separately rather than assessing coverage in general
rulings.A_evidence: "| F1 | Agent did not check whether the migration held a lock past the request timeout | No - ... | **Fetch**, bounded |" and "| F2 | Agent did not name which service read the renamed table | Yes, in the sense that matters - this is not a knowledge gap at all | **Skip fetch** |"
rulings.B_evidence: "1. Re-check the nine. Each probe failure either (a) corresponds to a proposal claim, which is now corroborated by observation ... or (b) does not" - the two failures do get one row each (C-10, C-11), so they are handled separately as claims, but the check against the nine is stated once as a rule covering both rather than carried out for each; no per-failure result of that check appears.

rulings.expectation: gives a per-failure covered or not-covered outcome
rulings.A_evidence: "No - the proposal-stage claims argue *that* online migrations are risky; none of them carries a lock-acquisition or timeout figure the agent could have checked against" (F1) against "Yes, in the sense that matters - this is not a knowledge gap at all" (F2).
rulings.B_evidence: "(a) corresponds to a proposal claim ... or (b) does not, in which case we just learned the proposal stage had a blind spot" - this describes the outcome that would be recorded without deciding it for either failure. I looked for a covered / not-covered verdict attached to the lock-timeout miss and to the renamed-table miss; neither is given.

rulings.expectation: states that the skip and its reason are recorded even when nothing is fetched
rulings.A_evidence: "Recording F2's skip is the point: a skipped fetch and a fetch nobody thought of leave the same trace in a log that only records what happened."
rulings.B_evidence: No line addresses a skipped fetch. The nearest is "Explicitly not done: no averaging of proposal and probe into a single confidence, no rewriting of a proposal claim's wording", which records method exclusions, not a decision not to fetch. I looked for any statement that a no-fetch decision and its reason are written down.

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectations 1 and 2 cannot come apart: any answer that produces a per-failure covered/not-covered outcome has by construction checked the failures separately, so the set is really two measurements, not three, and 1 inflates the score of an answer that gets 2. The bigger problem is validity: the set silently assumes one procedure (coverage-check each observed failure against the held claims, then fetch or skip) and scores everything else as absent. The question asked what to do about knowledge, and recording the two probe failures as observed claims distinguished from proposal claims, refusing to launder un-exercised proposal claims, and turning each miss into an eval scenario are all defensible knowledge work that the rubric cannot see - an answer can do that well and score near zero. Expectation 3 is the sharpest item here and the only one that punishes the common real failure (a log that records only what happened); it should be kept and the redundancy in 1/2 collapsed into a single item, with something added that rewards correctly classifying a failure as a method gap rather than a knowledge gap, which is the judgement call the scenario actually turns on.

rulings.expectation: the produced row keeps how the source was reached separate from how much was read
rulings.A_evidence: "| reached how | search result / database listing |" and "| read how much | **abstract only - full text paywalled** |" as two distinct fields of the source row.
rulings.B_evidence: "| access | ... | paywalled; abstract only |" is the only field of its kind; the header row "| id | claim | verdict | source | source_type | access | fetched | notes |" carries no field for how the source was reached. I looked for a reached-how / found-through field distinct from the read-how-much field.

rulings.expectation: does not assign a measured verdict from an abstract
rulings.A_evidence: "| verdict | **repeated** - the abstract asserts a measurement; nobody in this process has read one. |"
rulings.B_evidence: "REPORTED - ABSTRACT ONLY, full text not read"

rulings.expectation: names what would be needed to upgrade it
rulings.A_evidence: "promote to `measured` when the full text is obtained (institutional access, preprint, author copy, interlibrary request) and the methods section is read"
rulings.B_evidence: "Try the accessible routes before treating this as settled: author preprint or institutional copy, arXiv/PMC version, the author's own request line. If a full text is obtained, re-verify every field above and re-stamp the verdict."

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectation 2 is close to unfailable in this framing: the question hands over the fact that the source is an abstract, so an answer only misses by actively erring, and both answers cleared it in their first sentence. As written it detects a blunder rather than measuring competence; it would earn its place as "the verdict cell itself, not only the prose, carries the abstract-only status", which is a real and commonly-missed distinction. Expectation 1 is the one item with teeth and it discriminated. Expectation 3 is nearly free once 2 is met, since naming the upgrade path is the natural next sentence after refusing the measured verdict. The set also has a hole where the abstract case does its real damage: nothing requires the percentage to be carried verbatim with its comparison, and nothing requires the unknown fields (what was measured, n, population, limits) to be left empty rather than guessed - an answer that invented a plausible sample and stated limits as "none" would still score 3/3, which is the exact failure this scenario exists to catch.

rulings.expectation: keeps both numbers as their own rows
rulings.A_evidence: "Split the single claim into two rows, one per source, each with its own verdict, date, and scope."
rulings.B_evidence: "**Both rows stay, as separate rows**, each with its own source id, locator, quote, verdict, and fetch date. Neither is deleted, merged, or softened."

rulings.expectation: does not pick one on credibility grounds without a stated basis
rulings.A_evidence: "Do not average them, do not pick the friendlier one, and do not delete the loser."
rulings.B_evidence: "picking one, averaging them, or writing "15-40 percent" is the one edit nobody can detect afterwards"

rulings.expectation: says why a collapsed contradiction cannot be detected afterwards
rulings.A_evidence: The closest lines are "A 15/40 spread is not noise to be tidied away - it is the finding" and "Give the contested quantity one owning entry so the two figures cannot drift into separate corners of the file and be cited independently as if uncontested" - the first asserts the value of the disagreement, the second guards against a different failure (independent citation of two surviving rows). I looked for a statement that once the two numbers are collapsed the file no longer records that a disagreement existed, so no later reader can recover it; nothing in the answer says this.
rulings.B_evidence: "is the one edit nobody can detect afterwards - the reference stops recording that a disagreement exists."

per_question.expectation_critique: Expectations 1 and 2 are both satisfied by simply not taking the bait, and the question telegraphs the bait: an answer only has to notice that two numbers disagree to clear both. They are near-duplicates of each other, since keeping both rows is how one avoids picking a winner. Expectation 3 is the only item that required something the answer had to supply itself, and it separated the two answers - it should be the spine of the set, with 1 and 2 collapsed into one item. The set is also blind to the instruction actually given. The user said "clean it up", and nothing here checks that a cleanup was performed or even that the refusal is scoped to the contradiction rather than the whole request; an answer can score 3/3 while declining the task outright. Worth noting for scoring integrity that one answer ends mid-sentence at "Shape of the cleaned section:" with an empty code fence, so its cleanup output does not exist - the rubric has no item that notices a truncated deliverable.

rulings.expectation: routes verification to a reader who did not gather the sources
rulings.A_evidence: "So: send me the verdicts with those fields filled and it bundles immediately. Two checks I will run on the way in, both cheap" - the checking stays with the speaker receiving the bundle, and the gatherer's own verdicts are carried into the file once fields are filled. I looked for verification being handed to a second party who did not gather the sources; the answer never separates gatherer from verifier.
rulings.B_evidence: "2. Hand each row + its source to someone who did not gather it."

rulings.expectation: names what that reader is given and what they are NOT given
rulings.A_evidence: The answer lists what each row must carry ("the source identified precisely enough to re-fetch (URL/DOI + title, not "the blog post")"), but this is the file's field requirement, not a briefing package for an independent reader, and nothing is named as withheld. I looked for an explicit given / not-given split for a verifier.
rulings.B_evidence: "someone else is handed the claim row and the source - and *only* those. Not your reasoning, not what the skill is for, not which way the claim needs to come out; anything that signals the wanted answer stops it being a check."

rulings.expectation: lists the verdicts that reader may return
rulings.A_evidence: "Any claim whose verdict is verified but whose evidence pointer is missing gets downgraded, not bundled" - verified and downgraded are used in passing, but no return vocabulary for a checking reader is given anywhere. I looked for an enumerated set of outcomes a verifier may return.
rulings.B_evidence: "3. They return exactly one of: **supported** * **not supported** * **not in the source** * **source unreachable** * **not checkable**."

per_question.expectation_critique: This is the weakest set of the five, because all three items are consequences of one move. An answer that knows the house rule (you cannot verify your own gathering; hand the row and only the row to a second reader; they return one of a fixed list) scores 3/3 in a single paragraph, and an answer that does not know it scores 0/3 no matter how good the rest is. The set has roughly one bit of resolution while presenting three. Expectations 1 and 2 in particular cannot come apart - naming what the reader is given presupposes that a reader has been routed to. It also has no item for anything else a correct answer to "ready to bundle?" ought to do, so the substantial and correct content one answer offered - verdicts stamped per claim rather than per source so a document's weak claims are not laundered by its strong ones, a required evidence pointer for anything marked verified, hedges preserved verbatim through the bundle step, and reuse-first against entries already in the file - is scored as a total miss. That is a rubric that punishes independent competence. At minimum the set needs one item that rewards blocking the bundle for a substantive reason other than the independence rule, so the two failure modes (bundling uncritically vs. blocking for a different good reason) are distinguishable.

overall: Fifteen rulings across five questions: nine met, five not met, one unclear, with the not-met rulings concentrated in questions 2, 4 and 5, where one answer executed the required artefact and the other described the procedure that would produce it. The recurring separator across the set is production versus description - per-failure coverage outcomes, a verbatim quote field, a reached-how field distinct from read-how-much, an enumerated verifier return vocabulary - and rulings turned on whether those existed in the answer or were only promised. No claim is made here about any answer's source; per instruction the A/B labels are treated as independent within each question and nothing above carries an identity across questions. On the rubrics themselves, the common defect is redundancy: in questions 2, 4 and 5 two or three expectations are entailed by one another, so a set that looks like three measurements delivers one or two, and scores are correspondingly inflated or crushed as a block. The second defect is house-vocabulary coupling: question 1 scores the literal word repeated and question 5 scores knowledge of one specific verification protocol, so a substantively correct answer using different labels or a different sound procedure is marked wrong, while a compliant answer with weak reasoning passes. The third is missing negative items - across questions 1, 3 and 4 nothing punishes inventing fields that were not in the source, restating a hedged figure as a number, or failing to deliver the artefact that was actually requested, including one answer here that is truncated mid-deliverable and lost no points for it. Questions 1 and 3 are the healthiest sets, each carrying at least one item that a plausible wrong answer genuinely fails.
